opus-5.5.text:
I think endogenous reward is one of the most interesting and least understood questions right now.

Most of what we do in reinforcement learning today uses exogenous reward. Someone outside the agent defines what "good" means: you solved the math problem, you passed the unit tests, you won the game. That has worked remarkably well, especially for reasoning models, because in math or coding you can verify the answer. But it has a ceiling. The agent can only become as good as the reward functions we know how to write, and only in domains where we know how to write them.

Endogenous reward asks a different question: can the agent generate its own sense of what's worth doing, of progress, of whether it's getting better? Humans do this all the time. A child playing with blocks isn't being scored by anyone. A researcher working on a problem for years gets almost no external feedback, maybe a paper acceptance once in a while. What keeps them going is curiosity, a feeling of understanding something more deeply, a sense that one idea is more elegant than another. Those signals come from inside.

To me there are a few layers. The first is curiosity or novelty: wanting to explore what you don't yet understand. People have studied this in RL for a long time, but it's often fragile, like the "noisy TV" problem, where the agent just stares at randomness. The second layer is closer to self-evaluation: can the model judge its own work, notice a bad proof, feel that an explanation doesn't quite hold together? Language models can already do some of this, which is why I think it's a more promising time to revisit the idea. The third layer is more about values or goals: having something like long-term intentions that organize what counts as rewarding at all.

The reason I think this matters is the move toward agents that work over long horizons in the real world. If you want an agent to do something like research, or to run for weeks on an open-ended task, you can't hand-design a reward for every step, and the final outcome may be very far away or ambiguous. So either the agent learns to generate meaningful intermediate signals itself, or it gets stuck.

Of course there's a real risk too. Once the reward comes from inside the system, you have to ask whether it stays connected to what humans actually want, or whether it drifts or gets hacked. So I see endogenous reward not just as a capability question but also as a question about how the system's internal motivations relate to the external world and to people. I don't think anyone has fully figured that out yet, and that's partly why it's so exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
Endogenous reward, to me, is a reward signal that comes from inside the system rather than being handed to it from the outside. Traditional reinforcement learning has an environment that tells you "you scored a point" or "you solved the puzzle." That's exogenous. The reward is defined by someone else, and the agent just chases it.

But if you look at how humans actually learn, most of our rewards are internal. Curiosity, a sense that something is interesting, the feeling that you've understood something, discomfort when two of your beliefs contradict each other. Nobody gives you a score for those. They emerge from your own model of the world and your own goals.

For language models, I think there are a few layers to this. The simplest version is self-verification: the model generates a solution and then checks it, and the check itself becomes a training signal. A more interesting version is when the model's own uncertainty or surprise becomes the reward. If a prediction is wildly off, that's information worth pursuing. And the deepest version is when the model has its own objectives that it can decompose into subgoals and evaluate progress on, without someone having to label every step.

Why does this matter? Because exogenous reward doesn't scale. Every new task needs a new reward function, a new verifier, a new set of human labels. If we want agents that can operate in open-ended environments, the kind where no one has pre-written the scoring rules, they have to be able to generate their own sense of what counts as progress.

The honest caveat is that endogenous reward is also where the hard alignment questions live. If the model decides what's rewarding, you need to be very careful that its internal notion of "good" lines up with ours. So I'm excited about it as a direction, but I don't think it's a free lunch.

astra-6.text:
I think of endogenous reward as a reward signal that comes from the agent itself, rather than being supplied directly by the environment. For example, an external reward might tell you whether you solved a problem. An endogenous reward might reflect whether you learned something, reduced your uncertainty, or made progress toward a goal you set yourself.

The interesting question is how those internal signals relate to the external objective. Curiosity can motivate you to explore when there is no immediate payoff. But if you reward novelty alone, you can also become distracted by things that are surprising but useless. So having an internal reward is not automatically enough to produce useful behavior.

For language agents, one possible form is self-evaluation: the agent looks at its own actions and judges whether it is making progress. That can provide feedback when external feedback is sparse. But generating a judgment and generating a reliable judgment are different things. Ultimately, I think endogenous reward needs some grounding in interaction with the environment. Otherwise, the agent may just get better at convincing itself that it has succeeded.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of endogenous reward as a reward that comes from within the agent, rather than being supplied directly by the environment. You might solve a puzzle because someone pays you, but you might also solve it simply because you’re curious. That curiosity gives you a reason to act even when there’s no immediate external payoff.

For an AI agent, the interesting question is how to turn that into a useful learning signal. You could reward novelty, reducing uncertainty, or making progress on something the agent previously couldn’t do. But those are different things. If you reward novelty alone, the agent might keep watching random noise—it’s always surprising, but there’s nothing useful to learn. So I find learning progress a more compelling intuition: seek experiences that help you become more capable.

And I don’t think “endogenous” has to mean that the reward appears out of nowhere. The mechanism can still be designed or learned through interaction with an external objective. What makes it endogenous is that, during action, the agent can generate intermediate motivations for itself instead of waiting for someone to score every step.
